collection: SAT Reading and Writing original skill-focused practice
note: Eight original items per domain, with one question per wholly original stimulus. This equal-domain practice batch is not an official module blueprint, adaptive test or calibrated difficulty set. Eleven finer author-proposed skill mappings remain pending independent review. Model studies, people and data are illustrative rather than claims of published research. Word counts are whitespace editorial counts, not the framework’s exact six-character measure.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Identify a text’s central claim or a supported detail.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea?
questions.passage: When a neighbourhood archive began recording recipes, volunteers first collected ingredient lists. They soon found that cooks explained quantities through gestures and comparisons rather than fixed measurements. The archive therefore added short videos to its written records, preserving not only what went into a dish but also how cooks judged its preparation.
options: Written recipes are always more reliable than demonstrations.
Recording practical judgement required the archive to supplement ingredient lists with video.
The archive abandoned all written records when it discovered differences between cooks.
Fixed measurements prevented volunteers from collecting any useful information.
questions.answer: Recording practical judgement required the archive to supplement ingredient lists with video.
questions.explanation: The shift to video preserves gestures and judgements that ingredient lists alone omit. The text neither rejects writing entirely nor claims all cooks require fixed measurements.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Identify a text’s central claim or a supported detail.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes Imani’s attitude toward the station?
questions.passage: At the railway station, Imani kept a drawer of tickets from places she had never visited. Visitors assumed she longed to leave. Yet when a neighbour offered her a journey, she stayed to repair the station clock. The tickets, she said, reminded her that people could move through a place without making it less worth tending.
options: She considers it merely an obstacle to travelling.
She resents visitors because they misunderstand her collection.
She values caring for it while recognising the possibilities represented by travel.
She believes that repairing the clock will allow her to visit every place on the tickets.
questions.answer: She values caring for it while recognising the possibilities represented by travel.
questions.explanation: Her decision to repair the clock and her final remark connect openness to travel with care for the place where she lives. No plan to visit every destination is stated.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Select textual evidence that directly supports or tests a claim.
questions.prompt: Which finding would most directly support the explanation?
questions.passage: A theatre director claims that moving rehearsals into the performance hall helped actors adjust their voices to its unusual acoustics. The actors had previously rehearsed in a small classroom. A student is considering evidence that would specifically support the director’s explanation rather than merely show that the actors enjoyed the new location.
options: The hall had more comfortable chairs than the classroom.
Most actors preferred rehearsing in the evening.
After rehearsing in the hall, actors adjusted volume appropriately without repeated reminders about echoes.
The theatre’s posters used the same design before and after the move.
questions.answer: After rehearsing in the hall, actors adjusted volume appropriately without repeated reminders about echoes.
questions.explanation: Independent voice adjustments to the hall’s echoes directly connect the new location to acoustic adaptation; comfort, preferences and poster design do not.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Select textual evidence that directly supports or tests a claim.
questions.prompt: Which record would provide the strongest support for the claim?
questions.passage: A historian argues that a town’s old footbridge remained important after a road bridge opened nearby. The claim concerns continued practical use, not the footbridge’s age or appearance. Several records survive from the decade following the road bridge’s opening, but they differ in how directly they reveal travel behaviour.
options: A painting showing the footbridge before the road bridge was built.
A list of the kinds of wood used in the footbridge’s original construction.
A series of delivery logs showing regular crossings of the footbridge after the road bridge opened.
A poem praising the river without mentioning either bridge.
questions.answer: A series of delivery logs showing regular crossings of the footbridge after the road bridge opened.
questions.explanation: Post-opening crossing records directly document continuing use. Earlier construction information or artistic praise cannot establish that later practical role.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Integrate a short text with an original table to select supported evidence.
questions.prompt: Which statement best uses the table to support the claim?
questions.passage:
In a fictional trial, a library recorded the percentage of returned items that needed minor repairs. Books had the same binding type and were inspected under the same rule. A student claims that protective sleeves were associated with fewer repairs in both branches. The table reports percentages, not the numbers of books inspected.

| Branch | Without sleeve | With sleeve |
|---|---:|---:|
| East | 18% | 7% |
| West | 12% | 8% |
options: East inspected exactly eleven more books than West.
Both branches had identical repair percentages with sleeves.
Sleeves eliminated every repair in both branches.
Repair percentages fell from 18% to 7% in East and from 12% to 8% in West with sleeves.
questions.answer: Repair percentages fell from 18% to 7% in East and from 12% to 8% in West with sleeves.
questions.explanation: Both rows show lower repair percentages with sleeves. Percentages alone do not give inspected-book counts, and neither rate falls to zero.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Integrate a short text with an original table to select supported evidence.
questions.prompt: Which observation best supports the students’ prediction?
questions.passage:
A classroom model compares the time needed to complete two indexing tasks by hand and with a new tool. Students predict that the tool will save more time on a larger collection. They measure total completion time, including setup, rather than the rate of processing only after setup is finished.

| Collection | By hand | With tool |
|---|---:|---:|
| Small | 24 min | 20 min |
| Large | 90 min | 56 min |
options: The tool saves four minutes for the small collection but thirty-four minutes for the large one.
The tool takes longer than hand indexing for both collections.
The hand method takes less time for the large collection than for the small one.
The tool eliminates setup time for both collections.
questions.answer: The tool saves four minutes for the small collection but thirty-four minutes for the large one.
questions.explanation: The larger absolute saving is 90−56=34 minutes, compared with 24−20=4 minutes. Nothing in the table separates setup from later processing.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Draw a warranted inference without extending beyond the text.
questions.prompt: Which inference is best supported?
questions.passage: A translator kept two versions of a story’s opening sentence. One preserved the original word order but sounded stiff in the new language; the other changed the order while retaining the same relationships among the characters. She selected the second version after reading both aloud to listeners who had not seen the original.
options: The listeners were able to compare the new version directly with the original language.
The translator considered how the sentence worked for its new audience, rather than treating original word order as decisive.
The translator believed that character relationships could be changed without affecting the story.
The selected version was shorter than the original.
questions.answer: The translator considered how the sentence worked for its new audience, rather than treating original word order as decisive.
questions.explanation: The choice and audience test show attention to the new-language reading experience while preserving relationships. Listener knowledge, length and permission to change relationships are unsupported.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Draw a warranted inference without extending beyond the text.
questions.prompt: What does the student’s revision most strongly suggest?
questions.passage: A student botanist expected every plant beside a stream to have deeper roots than plants on the nearby slope. Her measurements showed substantial overlap between the two groups. She retained the individual results and revised her report to discuss variation within each location instead of describing a sharp division.
options: She discarded the plants that did not match her expectation.
The stream and slope plants had identical roots in every respect.
The measuring instrument could not distinguish any root lengths.
She treated the data as a reason to qualify an initially simple expectation.
questions.answer: She treated the data as a reason to qualify an initially simple expectation.
questions.explanation: Keeping overlapping measurements and revising the sharp distinction show qualification of the hypothesis, not discarded data or proof that all roots were identical.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Determine a word’s meaning from its specific context.
questions.prompt: As used in the text, “spare” most nearly means
questions.passage: The composer’s manuscript contains several spare passages. In these sections, a single instrument repeats a short phrase while the rest of the ensemble remains silent. Rather than filling every pause, the composer allows the isolated notes and the spaces between them to carry the musical argument.
options: simple and unadorned.
available for replacement.
unexpectedly cheerful.
damaged and incomplete.
questions.answer: simple and unadorned.
questions.explanation: A single instrument and deliberate silences establish restrained simplicity, not a backup passage or damage.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Determine a word’s meaning from its specific context.
questions.prompt: As used in the text, “material” most nearly means
questions.passage: The engineer did not dismiss the residents’ complaints as incidental. Although the bridge met the required load standard, the vibrations made pedestrians uneasy. She regarded those reports as material to the redesign and included them alongside the instrument readings when comparing possible changes to the structure.
options: made of cloth.
relevant and significant.
difficult to transport.
already settled.
questions.answer: relevant and significant.
questions.explanation: The reports matter to the redesign alongside measured data, so material means relevant or significant.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Determine a word’s meaning from its specific context.
questions.prompt: As used in the text, “qualified” most nearly means
questions.passage: A critic described the novelist’s early popularity as a qualified success. The book reached many readers, but its hurried publication left passages that the author later revised substantially. The critic therefore distinguished the achievement of finding an audience from the separate achievement of producing a fully resolved work.
options: limited by reservations.
supported by professional training.
open only to approved readers.
proven beyond any doubt.
questions.answer: limited by reservations.
questions.explanation: The success is acknowledged but restricted by concern over unfinished passages; qualifications here are reservations, not credentials.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a textual element contributes to a rhetorical purpose.
questions.prompt: What is the main function of the account of the young tree?
questions.passage: A report on urban trees begins by noting that planting totals are easy to count. It then follows one young tree through watering, pruning and replacement of damaged supports over several years. The report ends by proposing that cities track long-term tree survival as well as the number initially planted.
options: To show that all urban trees require replacement every year.
To establish that counting is impossible in environmental projects.
To argue that pruning matters more than every other form of care.
To illustrate the continuing work obscured by an initial planting total.
questions.answer: To illustrate the continuing work obscured by an initial planting total.
questions.explanation: The multi-year account motivates tracking survival and care beyond an easily counted planting event.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a textual element contributes to a rhetorical purpose.
questions.prompt: Why does the historian mention tax-exempt traders?
questions.passage: In a short essay, a historian first presents a tax register as evidence of a busy market. She then notes that traders exempt from the tax would not appear in it. Finally, she compares the register with private correspondence. The qualification does not make the register useless; it clarifies what its silence can mean.
options: To prove that the market had no permanent traders.
To claim that every private letter records trade accurately.
To identify a limitation that makes comparison with another source valuable.
To replace the tax register with a complete list of residents.
questions.answer: To identify a limitation that makes comparison with another source valuable.
questions.explanation: Exempt traders reveal a gap in the register, motivating the use of correspondence without rejecting the register altogether.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a textual element contributes to a rhetorical purpose.
questions.prompt: What role does the final sentence play?
questions.passage: Mara counted the empty flowerpots before opening the shop. Yesterday she had counted the coins in the till; tomorrow, she thought, she would count the seedlings that had survived the cold. The narrator’s attention to these small inventories follows Mara as she begins to measure the business by something other than its daily sales.
options: It reveals that Mara has stopped selling plants.
It gives instructions for protecting seedlings from cold weather.
It interprets the changing focus of the inventories described earlier.
It explains why the shop’s accounts are numerically incorrect.
questions.answer: It interprets the changing focus of the inventories described earlier.
questions.explanation: The sentence connects coins, pots and surviving seedlings to Mara’s changing idea of what matters in the business.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Compare related texts and identify agreement or response.
questions.prompt: How would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Text 1?
questions.passage:
Text 1: A digital catalogue makes a collection searchable from far away. For many researchers, that access removes the need for an initial journey simply to learn what the archive holds.

Text 2: Searchability is valuable, but catalogue descriptions may omit marks on the objects themselves. Some research questions therefore still require direct examination of the collection.
options: By denying that catalogues can be searched from outside an archive.
By arguing that every researcher must travel before choosing a topic.
By claiming that physical objects contain no information beyond their catalogue entries.
By agreeing that remote catalogues help researchers while noting that some questions still require examining physical objects.
questions.answer: By agreeing that remote catalogues help researchers while noting that some questions still require examining physical objects.
questions.explanation: Text 2 acknowledges access but distinguishes discovery from research needing physical details. Text 1’s narrower benefit is compatible with that limit.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Compare related texts and identify agreement or response.
questions.prompt: Which idea would both authors most likely accept?
questions.passage:
Text 1: When small shops share delivery vehicles, each shop can receive goods without arranging a separate trip. This coordination may reduce the number of vehicles serving the same street.

Text 2: Shared deliveries are most effective when shops can agree on timing. If their schedules are incompatible, vehicles may still need repeated visits, reducing the expected advantage.
options: Shared delivery systems always require more vehicles than separate deliveries.
Timing has no bearing on delivery arrangements.
Coordinated deliveries can offer advantages, though the arrangement’s operation matters.
Every shop on a street must sell the same products before sharing is possible.
questions.answer: Coordinated deliveries can offer advantages, though the arrangement’s operation matters.
questions.explanation: Both allow a benefit from coordination; Text 2 specifies a condition affecting its size. Neither asserts a universal gain or a same-product requirement.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Select a transition that expresses the relationship between ideas.
questions.prompt: Which transition most logically completes the text?
questions.passage: The first edition of the guide listed buildings by the dates when they were completed. The revised edition groups them by the purposes they served, such as trade, worship or education. ___, a reader looking for market buildings can now find them together instead of searching through several centuries of entries.
options: Nevertheless
Similarly
As a result
Previously
questions.answer: As a result
questions.explanation: Grouping by purpose causes market buildings to appear together, so a consequence transition is needed.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Select a transition that expresses the relationship between ideas.
questions.prompt: Which transition most logically completes the text?
questions.passage: The two maps use the same colours for rivers, roads and woodland, making their legends look nearly identical. ___, they represent very different scales: a centimetre on the first covers a village, while a centimetre on the second covers an entire province. Readers must therefore check more than the colour key.
options: Likewise
However
Consequently
For example
questions.answer: However
questions.explanation: The text contrasts similar colour systems with different scales; scale does not follow as a consequence of the colours.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Select a transition that expresses the relationship between ideas.
questions.prompt: Which transition best introduces the shared purpose?
questions.passage: The workshop’s first session asks participants to identify a tool by touch while keeping it hidden from view. The second asks them to describe a familiar object without naming it. ___, both exercises make participants attend to features they might otherwise take for granted during ordinary use.
options: Instead
Earlier
Conversely
In both cases
questions.answer: In both cases
questions.explanation: In both cases signals a shared purpose despite the exercises’ different methods.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Select a transition that expresses the relationship between ideas.
questions.prompt: Which transition most logically introduces the final sentence?
questions.passage: A researcher found that a list of subscribers could reveal more than the total audience for a magazine. It could also show connections among towns. ___, several subscribers in distant places used the same bookseller’s address, suggesting a distribution link that a simple readership count would overlook.
options: On the contrary
For instance
Nevertheless
Meanwhile
questions.answer: For instance
questions.explanation: The common bookseller address is a concrete example of the geographical connections the list can reveal.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Use supplied notes to fulfil a stated rhetorical goal.
questions.prompt: The student wants to explain how the portable stage solves an access problem. Which choice best uses the notes?
questions.passage:
A student has gathered these notes:
- A group built a portable stage from sections that fit into a small van.
- Each section can be carried by two people.
- The stage can be assembled in courtyards with limited vehicle access.
- A fixed stage in the same district cannot be moved.
- Both stages host performances by local musicians.
options: Because its sections fit in a small van and can be carried, the portable stage can reach courtyards that are difficult for vehicles to enter.
Both the fixed and portable stages host local musicians.
A fixed stage can be moved between courtyards whenever musicians need it.
The district’s musicians prefer large vehicles to small vans.
questions.answer: Because its sections fit in a small van and can be carried, the portable stage can reach courtyards that are difficult for vehicles to enter.
questions.explanation: The correct choice links portability and carrying to constrained courtyard access. The other accurate similarity does not meet the stated goal, and the remaining claims contradict or exceed the notes.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Use supplied notes to fulfil a stated rhetorical goal.
questions.prompt: The student wants to emphasise the researchers’ common aim rather than their different sources. Which choice best achieves that goal?
questions.passage:
A student has gathered these notes:
- Researcher A examined drawings of a wetland made over fifty years.
- Researcher B compared dated photographs of the same wetland.
- Both researchers traced changes in the water’s edge.
- The drawings contain annotations by their makers.
- The photographs include a visible measuring post in some years.
options: Drawings may include annotations, whereas some photographs show a measuring post.
Both researchers used historical records to trace changes in the wetland’s water edge.
One researcher used drawings spanning fifty years.
The measuring post proves that drawings cannot record water levels.
questions.answer: Both researchers used historical records to trace changes in the wetland’s water edge.
questions.explanation: Tracing the changing edge is the shared aim; source-specific features do not foreground it, and the final assertion is unsupported.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Use supplied notes to fulfil a stated rhetorical goal.
questions.prompt: The student wants to clarify the relationship between the fabric and the finished artwork. Which choice best uses the notes?
questions.passage:
A student has gathered these notes:
- A sculptor makes a sequence of bowls from the same clay.
- The sculptor presses different woven fabrics against the wet surfaces.
- The fabric is removed before firing.
- Its pattern remains as a texture in the fired clay.
- No fabric is part of the finished bowls.
options: The bowls are woven from fabric after the clay has been fired.
The finished bowls retain both clay and fabric as permanent materials.
The fabric leaves a texture in the clay but is removed before firing, so it is a tool for forming the surface rather than a component of the finished bowl.
Every woven fabric produces the same texture on the bowls.
questions.answer: The fabric leaves a texture in the clay but is removed before firing, so it is a tool for forming the surface rather than a component of the finished bowl.
questions.explanation: The correct choice integrates the retained impression and removed fabric, accurately distinguishing tool from final material.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Use supplied notes to fulfil a stated rhetorical goal.
questions.prompt: The student wants to explain what the interviews added to the archive. Which choice best achieves that goal?
questions.passage:
A student has gathered these notes:
- An oral-history project recorded accounts from retired boatbuilders.
- The archive already held plans showing boat dimensions.
- Interviews described how builders chose timber and adjusted plans during construction.
- Some decisions were made by judging individual pieces of wood.
- The plans did not record those judgements.
options: The archive’s plans included boat dimensions.
The interviews documented practical decisions about timber and construction that the existing dimensional plans did not record.
Retired boatbuilders took part in an oral-history project.
Boat plans were discarded because dimensions were no longer useful.
questions.answer: The interviews documented practical decisions about timber and construction that the existing dimensional plans did not record.
questions.explanation: The correct choice states the additional kind of knowledge and contrasts it with what plans already supplied.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Edit punctuation and clause boundaries in context.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to Standard English conventions?
questions.passage: Artist Lami uses a technique ___ she layers translucent paper to produce colours that change as the viewer moves. The workshop notes explain that each layer remains partly visible, so the final effect depends on the interaction of several sheets rather than on one opaque surface.
options: called layering;
called layering,
called; layering,
called, layering;
questions.answer: called layering;
questions.explanation: Called layering completes the noun phrase and the first independent clause; the semicolon then joins it to the independent clause beginning she. The comma choice creates a comma splice.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Edit punctuation and clause boundaries in context.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to Standard English conventions?
questions.passage: The restored courtyard—once used for storing broken equipment___ now hosts evening readings. Volunteers repaired its benches and planted shade trees, but they retained the uneven stones because residents considered them part of the site’s history. The redesign thus introduced a new purpose while preserving visible traces of the old one.
options: and
questions.explanation: The nonessential phrase opened by an em dash needs a closing em dash before the main verb now hosts.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Edit punctuation and clause boundaries in context.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to Standard English conventions?
questions.passage: The researchers labelled each jar with a code that identified its collection site. They also recorded the collection date ___ the code alone did not distinguish samples gathered at the same place in different seasons. Both pieces of information were needed to reconstruct the sequence of the study.
options: , because,
because;
because:
because
questions.answer: because
questions.explanation: Because correctly attaches the dependent explanation to the main clause. The other choices mispunctuate or detach that dependent clause.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Edit agreement, tense and modifiers in context.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to Standard English conventions?
questions.passage: The collection includes the work of two historians who shared one notebook during their survey. The ___ joint notes record street names, sketches and conversations with residents. A later editor used those entries to compare how the researchers divided their attention while walking the same route together.
options: historian’s
historians
historians’s
historians’
questions.answer: historians’
questions.explanation: Two historians jointly own the notes, requiring the plural possessive historians’. The singular possessive and nonpossessive forms do not fit.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Edit agreement, tense and modifiers in context.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to Standard English conventions?
questions.passage: The arrangement of narrow passages between the display cases ___ visitors slow down and view the objects from several angles. Designers chose this layout to encourage close observation rather than a quick walk through a single broad aisle, and they checked it with trial visits before opening.
options: makes
make
making
have made
questions.answer: makes
questions.explanation: The singular subject arrangement takes makes; the plural passages is inside a modifying phrase. Making lacks a finite main verb, and have made disagrees.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Edit agreement, tense and modifiers in context.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to Standard English conventions?
questions.passage: In 1948, the fictional town surveyor ___ a narrow path missing from the official map. Her report from that year described its use by residents travelling to the river and recommended adding it to the next edition. The discovery later helped historians compare official routes with everyday movement.
options: discovered
has discovered
discovering
will discover
questions.answer: discovered
questions.explanation: The completed event at a specified past time calls for discovered. Present perfect conflicts with that completed-time reference, the participle is not a finite predicate, and future tense conflicts with the report.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Edit agreement, tense and modifiers in context.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to Standard English conventions?
questions.passage: After examining the damaged bell, ___. They photographed the crack before beginning repairs, then compared its position with the original casting marks. This sequence allowed them to distinguish old features of the metal from changes that had occurred since the bell was installed.
options: a reinforcement of the rim was proposed by the conservators
the rim’s reinforcement became the conservators’ proposal
the damaged rim was proposed for reinforcement by the conservators
the conservators proposed reinforcing its rim
questions.answer: the conservators proposed reinforcing its rim
questions.explanation: The conservators are the people who examined the bell and therefore must be the subject immediately following the introductory modifier. In the other choices the modifier wrongly attaches to reinforcement or rim.

questions.subject: Reading and Writing
questions.learningObjective: Edit agreement, tense and modifiers in context.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to Standard English conventions?
questions.passage: Neither the original manuscript nor the revised edition ___ the author’s sketches. Instead, the publisher kept the drawings in a separate folder, where readers encountered them only when consulting the archive. The absence matters because several scenes in the story refer to places that the sketches depict in detail.
options: includes
include
including
have included
questions.answer: includes
questions.explanation: Both coordinated subjects are singular, so the finite verb includes agrees. Including leaves the clause without a finite verb, while include and have included are plural.
